summary:
Planet Hunter is a free public website that shows real images of the sky from NASA's SPHEREx telescope and makes it easy for anyone to see how they change over time. In SPHEREx's pictures the stars stay still, but the worlds of our Solar System move. Planet Hunter lets everyone see that for themselves, and try it.
Visitors fly from the Milky Way into a 3D Solar System where every world sits at its real NASA JPL position, then open the real SPHEREx pictures of ten worlds, from Uranus to distant Makemake. They can watch the sky change in four ways, one click each: blink two dates, play a time-lapse, compare the same sky six months apart, or turn a 3D time stack. Then they can hunt moving worlds the way astronomers do (detect, predict, classify), race an automatic detector, and fly a space mission that ends by stacking images to reveal a hidden planet, the method behind the real search for Planet Nine.
Every sky image is a real SPHEREx observation with a link to NASA's original file. On every visit the site checks NASA's servers to show whether it uses the latest data release, and one command rebuilds it when a new release comes out. It works on computers and phones, in English and Bahasa Malaysia, with a welcome guide, a Help page and a ready-made classroom lesson.
details:
Keeping up with NASA. SPHEREx data arrives in releases. On every visit the site asks NASA's servers which releases exist and shows whether its pictures use the latest one. Every week an automatic check on GitHub alerts the team when a new release appears, and one command searches it and rebuilds every picture, which a person checks before publishing.


Honesty. Every image shows its date, detector and wavelength, with a link to NASA's original file. The automatic detector is classic image subtraction, not machine learning, and its result is shown openly: its top pick is right for 7 of the 10 worlds, and it misses the two faintest. Simulated planets are always labelled, and the About page lists every simplification.


Benefits
Anyone can see real NASA data change, with no science background, no login and no software to install.


People learn how discoveries are really made: find it, predict it, classify it, and judge how far to trust a computer.


It reaches more people: free, on a phone, in Bahasa Malaysia as well as English, with a lesson ready for teachers.


It stays current as NASA releases more SPHEREx data.
Intended impact
SPHEREx images hundreds of millions of objects. Computers scan them, but people still need to understand what is being looked for and how far to trust the software. We want school pupils, teachers and the public, starting in Sarawak and Malaysia, to see that the sky changes, to understand how astronomers find moving worlds, and to feel that they could join the search, including the search for a Planet X.
How it meets each judging criterion


Impact: free, no login, works on a phone, in English and Bahasa Malaysia, with a ready-made lesson for teachers and a result card that invites friends to play.


Creativity: visitors do the astronomer's own job (find, predict, classify, race a machine, stack images to find a hidden planet), with new views of this data such as the 3D time stack.


Validity: every image is a real SPHEREx observation linked to NASA's original file, every position is checked against NASA JPL, and the detector's 7-of-10 score and all simplifications are stated openly.


Relevance: it is exactly the requested public web tool. It displays SPHEREx sky images, offers four one-click ways to see them change over time, and checks for new NASA releases on every visit.

Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), three.js for 3D, hosted on GitHub Pages


Data preparation: Python with Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow and Requests


Textures: Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0) and NASA/JHUAPL/SwRI (Pluto map)


Testing: automated play-throughs in a real browser, on computer and phone screen sizes, against the live site


What it cannot do
It does not search for new objects. Every world shown is already known.
It shows small prepared patches of sky, not the whole SPHEREx survey.
On-screen brightness and colours are adjusted so faint things show; they are not measurements.
The 3D Solar System enlarges the planets so they can be seen, and its Milky Way is a model. Positions and orbits are real.
The game's ship, debris and weapons are fiction. Its scanner pictures are real.
The front page's shooting stars, coloured haze and music are decoration.
